notes.body:
When Maulana Ali tells Kumayl that religion (دِين) is kin to debt (دَيْن), he is not making a clever pun — he is opening a door. Both words grow from **one root** holding a single idea: to be bound to another, to owe, and so to obey.

So what does our intellect owe? It owes the very gift that made it an intellect. Allah did not create the mind already full; He created it *able* to know and set it loose in the world. **That capacity is the loan** — a debt incurred at our origin, the moment we were given a mind that could reach for truth.

A loan is repaid by using it for what it was given for, and the mind was given so that it might come to know its Maker. Every act of real knowing, then, is a payment made:

- the faculty is first given in potential,
- knowledge turns that potential into something living and actual,
- and so the intellect returns to its Source exactly what its Source intended.

This is why the wise apprehension of knowledge (معرفة العلم) is called **a religion by which Allah is worshipped** — for to know is itself to obey.

إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ الْإِسْلَامُ  
"Truly, religion in the sight of Allah is submission."  
Al-Imran 3:19

Is this only wordplay, or a real claim about where the intellect comes from? It is **both at once** — the play on words is the vessel, and the truth it carries is about our very beginning. To know is not a favour we do for Allah; it is the quiet settling of a debt we have owed since we were made. And of all debts this is the sweetest to repay, for the more of it we return, the richer we grow.
notes.anchor: the debt his own intellect has incurred to its Maker
notes.quote: the debt his own intellect has incurred to its Maker
etymology: دَيْن (debt): from the root د-ي-ن, whose sense is to be under obligation to another. From it come دائن, the creditor, and مَدِين, the one who owes. To be in دَيْن is to hold something that is not finally your own until you give it back.

دِين (religion): from the same root د-ي-ن, which also carries the meanings of obeying, submitting, and following a binding way, and is kin to دَانَ, to judge or requite. So دِين names the whole bond of owing and answering to Allah — faith understood as a debt of the self.

عقل (intellect): from the root ع-ق-ل, to bind or tie, as a rope (عِقال) tethers a camel. The عقل is the faculty that binds scattered understanding into one, and binds the soul back toward its Maker — the very gift whose granting is what incurs the debt.

notes.body:
Return the SAME explanation, better articulated.

When Maulana Ali cried out that the earth will never be empty of one who establishes the proof of God, he was naming the rarest people alive. The **proof of God** — الحُجّة — is understood here as a living person, not a book or a clever argument, someone through whom Allah keeps His truth visible on the earth in every age.

In the reading the Ismaili tradition draws from this sermon, that living proof is first and foremost **the Imam**. Just as a courtroom needs a living judge and not merely a written law, Allah leaves in every age a rightly-guided guide, so that no soul can ever say the path was closed to it.

Beneath the Imam stand his **true friends** — the lordly knowers Maulana Ali calls عَالِم رَبَّانِيّ — who carry the same light in smaller lamps. These are sincere disciples like Kumayl himself, trusted to receive the inner knowledge and pass it only to hearts that resemble their own.

What makes someone a bearer of the proof is not learning stored in the head but knowledge that has **taken the heart**. Three marks are named for such a one:

- their bodies keep company with the world while their spirits are bound to the higher realm,
- they take hold of the very spirit of certainty,
- they entrust what they carry only to their true peers, never trading it for worldly gain.

This is why they are fewest in number yet **greatest in rank**. Truth here is never settled by a show of hands; a whole crowd can be astray while a single hidden witness keeps the proof of Allah alive. So when Maulana Ali sighed, "Ah, how I long to see them," he was longing for exactly these few — the ones through whom religion stays forever true to itself.
notes.anchor: one who establishes the proof of God
notes.quote: one who establishes the proof of God
etymology: حُجّة (proof): from the root ح-ج-ج, whose core sense is to aim or make for something — the same root that gives الحَجّ, the pilgrimage, a journey pointed at one goal. A حُجّة is therefore a decisive authority one is drawn toward, and in this sermon it is a living person rather than a mere argument.

رَبَّانِيّ (lordly): from ر-ب-ب, the root of رَبّ, the Lord who nurtures and raises what He owns. One who is رَبَّانِيّ belongs wholly to that Lord and is reared by Him — knowledge nursed by Allah rather than simply collected, which is why such a knower carries light and not only facts.

خَلِيفَة (vicegerent): from خ-ل-ف, to come after or to succeed. A خَلِيفَة is one who stands in the place of another and continues his work — here, one who represents Allah upon His earth, carrying His authority forward rather than holding any authority of his own.

notes.body:
The Greek word in play here is μάρτυς, which at first meant nothing more than a witness — a person who stands up and testifies to what they have truly seen, as in a court of law. When the early Christians held to their faith even unto death, that word took on a second life, and **a witness became a martyr**: one who testifies not with words alone but with their very blood.

The Arabic شهيد grows from an entirely different soil. It springs from the root ش-ه-د, to be present and to bear testimony, and from that one root come both the شهادة, the testimony of faith, and the شهيد, the one who seals that testimony with their life. So the same pair of meanings — witness and martyr — sits inside this single word, just as it does inside the Greek.

Is this a shared ancestry or only a meeting of minds? It is the second: **a parallel of meaning, never a shared root.**

- Greek belongs to one family of languages and Arabic to another; neither word descends from the other.
- What the two share is a pattern of meaning — a witness ripening into a martyr — that two traditions arrived at on their own.
- The writer reaches for the Greek only to light up the Arabic, not to trace a line of descent.

This is why the image moves us so in this passage. The true intellectual who storms his own ego and offers up his false life bears witness to Allah — and in that offering he is a martyr in the fullest sense. Both truths breathe within the one word شهيد, and becoming that word is exactly what the ethos of Maulana Ali asks of us.

notes.quote: meaning both martyr and witness, as in the original Greek sense of the word
etymology: شهيد (witness / martyr): from the root ش-ه-د, to be present and to testify to what one has seen. The same root gives شاهد, a witness, and شهادة, the act of testifying; the martyr is called شهيد because he testifies to the truth with his very life and stands present before Allah.

μάρτυς (witness): the Greek term that first named a legal witness and, through the early Christians who testified unto death, came to mean martyr. It is the source of the English word 'martyr' and the parallel that lights up شهيد — a likeness of meaning, not a shared origin.
